articles.title: I don't like passkeys
articles.summary: Passkeys are a technology that offers better security against man-in-the-middle attacks, but they also create a false sense of security and can lead to permanent account lockout, automated account bans, and device loss. Unlike traditional passwords, passkeys are asymmetric and cannot be recovered from the server-side details, making them a good fit for corporate environments but a poor fit for personal security. Additionally, hardware keys, which are used to create and manage passkeys, have limitations and can be expensive to purchase and maintain.

articles.title: Bend
articles.summary: Bend is a fast language that blocks AI mistakes via proof, providing an ambiguity-free way to tell AIs what we want done. It compiles to native code, runs nearly as fast as C on one core, and can run up to a hundred times faster than one core on the GPU. Bend's type checker is a proof checker, as in Lean and Rocq, and takes a second at most to check after every change, allowing AI agents to check after every change. This ensures that code is free from mistakes, making it ideal for applications where bug-free and fast performance are crucial.

articles.title: The scourge of x86 emulation
articles.summary: The scourge of x86 emulation affects every application that emulates x86, including those that use ARM's relaxed consistency model. This problem arises from the stark contrast between ARM's weak ordering model and x86's strict total store ordering model. The weak ordering model, which is the default for ARM, allows significant hardware optimizations but also introduces issues with coherence and visibility of memory loads and stores. This can lead to unexpected behavior and bugs in applications that rely on strict consistency and atomicity.
